nodes.statement: The talk's second part rests on the assumption that computers are a radical novelty, and the first part must define "radical" and give evidence for the assumption.
nodes.span: pursues some of the scientific and educational consequences of the assumption that computers represent a radical novelty
nodes.status_reason: stated as the talk's declared scope, not derived

nodes.statement: People habitually plan for the future using the vocabulary and concepts inherited from past experience, stretching them to fit.
nodes.span: The usual way in which we plan today for tomorrow is in yesterday's vocabulary
nodes.status_reason: offered as an observation the reader can check but not derived

nodes.statement: Linguists observe that word meanings evolve only slowly and gradually.
nodes.span: the meanings of words evolve over time, but also know that this is a slow and gradual process
nodes.status_reason: cited testimony, checkable but unsupported here

nodes.statement: Coping by metaphor and analogy works under slow, gradual change but breaks down under sharp discontinuity, where past experience is irrelevant and metaphors mislead.
nodes.span: in the case of a sharp discontinuity, however, the method breaks down
nodes.status_reason: follows from the habit of reusing old concepts plus the slowness of meaning-change

nodes.statement: A "radical" novelty is defined as one for which the analogy-to-the-familiar method fails.
nodes.span: This is the situation that is characteristic for the "radical" novelty.
nodes.status_reason: definition extracted from the breakdown case just described

nodes.statement: Radical novelty must be met by an orthogonal method: approaching it with a blank mind, as a dissociated topic, like learning an untranslatable foreign language.
nodes.span: Coping with radical novelty requires an orthogonal method
nodes.status_reason: follows from the inadequacy of the familiar established in n4/n5

nodes.statement: Because the orthogonal method requires hard work, adjusting to radical novelties is unpopular and the novelties themselves unwelcome.
nodes.span: adjusting to radical novelties is not a very popular activity, for it requires hard work
nodes.status_reason: derived from the effort demanded by n6

nodes.statement: Radical novelties are so disturbing that they tend to be suppressed, ignored, or even denied the possibility of existing.
nodes.span: radical novelties are so disturbing that they tend to be suppressed or ignored
nodes.status_reason: extends the unwelcomeness claim n7

nodes.statement: Gauss suppressed his discovery of non-Euclidean geometry out of fear, leaving Bolyai and Lobatchewsky to take the criticism.
nodes.span: he decided to suppress his discovery of non-Euclidean geometry
nodes.status_reason: historical instance offered without derivation

nodes.statement: The Middle Ages combined rampant reasoning by analogy with near-total intellectual stagnation, showing the two go together.
nodes.span: "reasoning by analogy" was rampant; another characteristic was almost total intellectual stagnation
nodes.status_reason: historical correlation asserted, mechanism not derived

nodes.statement: A very large fraction of the population treats gradual change as the only paradigm of history.
nodes.span: the fraction of the population for which gradual change seems to be all but the only paradigm of history is very large
nodes.status_reason: supported only by the speaker's own observation

nodes.statement: The speaker's own observation found the number of such people much larger than he had expected.
nodes.span: their number turned out to be much larger than I had expected
nodes.status_reason: personal testimony

nodes.statement: The mathematical community tacitly assumes that doing mathematics will always remain the same kind of mental activity.
nodes.span: never challenged its tacit assumption that doing mathematics will remain very much the same type of mental activity
nodes.status_reason: asserted example of the gradual-change paradigm

nodes.statement: Robbins argues by analogy with running that the human mind, unchanged for millennia and already at its limit, permits no quantum leap in mathematical ability.
nodes.span: The human mind is no different now from what it was five thousand years ago.
nodes.status_reason: direct quotation offered as evidence

nodes.statement: Robbins's own analogy backfires: as with travel, effective alternatives to brain-running may exist, so one should reduce brain use and calculate.
nodes.span: for going from A to B fast, there could now exist alternatives to running that are orders of magnitude more effective
nodes.status_reason: turned against the quoted analogy n14

nodes.statement: Robbins escapes the radical novelty by definitional fiat, refusing the name "doing mathematics" to any alternative.
nodes.span: exorcizing the danger of radical novelty by the simple device of adjusting his definitions to his needs
nodes.status_reason: reading of the quotation n14 under the denial thesis n8

nodes.statement: Prevailing educational practice takes imperceptible gradual change as its exclusive paradigm, constantly linking new material to the student's familiar world.
nodes.span: It is the prevailing educational practice, for which gradual, almost imperceptible, change seems to be the exclusive paradigm
nodes.status_reason: illustrated by examples, not derived

nodes.statement: Arithmetic teaching disguises "plus" as "and" and restricts examples to visible familiar objects, and introductory calculus is split into field-adorned versions.
nodes.span: the hideous arithmetic operator "plus" is carefully disguised by calling it "and"
nodes.status_reason: concrete instances supporting n17

nodes.statement: An educational practice that fails to prepare the next generation for radical novelty is a serious shortcoming.
nodes.span: I consider the failure of an educational practice to prepare the next generation for the phenomenon of radical novelties a serious shortcoming
nodes.status_reason: follows from n6 and n17 given that coping requires training

nodes.statement: The Rector of Cervera boasted of banishing "the dangerous novelty of thinking", and Spain's ensuing century of troubles justifies calling the shortcoming serious.
nodes.span: Spain's problems in the century that followed justify my characterization of the shortcoming as "serious"
nodes.status_reason: historical anecdote offered in support of n19

nodes.statement: Radical novelties matter now because science and technology inflict them on a public ill-prepared to cope.
nodes.span: while we are ill-prepared to cope with them, science and technology have now shown themselves expert at inflicting them upon us
nodes.status_reason: combines the ill-preparedness claims with the cited modern examples

nodes.statement: Relativity and quantum mechanics spawned quasi-scientific tracts, and the atom bomb and the pill are handled with profound inadequacy.
nodes.span: Earlier scientific examples are the theory of relativity and quantum mechanics
nodes.status_reason: examples offered in support of n21

nodes.statement: Automatic computers embody not one but two radical novelties, and only identifying them as such lets us identify the surrounding nonsense and mythology.
nodes.span: automatic computers embody not only one radical novelty but two of them
nodes.status_reason: the central contention, announced before its argument

nodes.statement: We cope with bigness by hierarchical decomposition, whose depth is a kind of logarithm of the ratio between the whole and the smallest parts.
nodes.span: the depth of a hierarchical decomposition is some sort of logarithm of the ratio of the "sizes"
nodes.status_reason: asserted with everyday examples; the logarithm relation is not derived for this reader

nodes.statement: Computing spans a baffling ratio, from a bit to hundreds of megabytes and from a microsecond to half an hour.
nodes.span: From a bit to a few hundred megabytes, from a microsecond to a half an hour of computing
nodes.status_reason: a stated magnitude of today's equipment

nodes.statement: The programmer is uniquely required to bridge that gigantic ratio with a single technology, thinking in conceptual hierarchies far deeper than any mind faced before.
nodes.span: his is the only discipline and profession in which such a gigantic ratio
nodes.status_reason: follows from the decomposition-depth claim n24 applied to the ratio n25

nodes.statement: The first radical novelty is that the computer demands unprecedentedly deep conceptual hierarchies, an intellectual challenge without historical precedent.
nodes.span: the automatic computer confronts us with a radically new intellectual challenge that has no precedent in our history
nodes.status_reason: derived from n26 together with the definition of radical novelty n5

nodes.statement: Believers in gradual change see a computer as merely a bigger, faster cash register, an analogy shallower than comparing a jet to a crawling baby.
nodes.span: an automatic computer is something like the familiar cash register, only somewhat bigger, faster, and more flexible
nodes.status_reason: instance of the denial thesis n8 applied to n27

nodes.statement: Almost all familiar mechanisms, including how we view ourselves, are analogue: behaviour is a continuous and often monotonic function of parameters.
nodes.span: the vast majority of our mechanisms are viewed as analogue devices whose behaviour is over a large range a continuous function
nodes.status_reason: supported by everyday examples the reader can check

nodes.statement: The second radical novelty is that the automatic computer is our first large-scale digital device.
nodes.span: the automatic computer is our first large-scale digital device
nodes.status_reason: stands on the near-absence of prior discrete mechanisms n29

nodes.statement: Viewing a program as a device is dangerous, because a single-bit perturbation can have drastic consequences, unlike any analogue device.
nodes.span: the smallest possible perturbations —i.e. changes of a single bit— can have the most drastic consequences
nodes.status_reason: follows from digital encoding n30 contrasted with continuity n29

nodes.statement: In computing there is and will be no meaningful metric in which small changes go with small effects.
nodes.span: there is no meaningful metric in which "small" changes and "small" effects go hand in hand
nodes.status_reason: generalization of the single-bit sensitivity n31

nodes.statement: Redundancy and error correction do not essentially change this picture.
nodes.span: the picture is not essentially changed by the introduction of redundancy or error correction
nodes.status_reason: asserted as a caveat without argument

nodes.statement: The second radical novelty is denied because its truth would be too discomforting, at a cost plausibly of a million dollars a day in the US.
nodes.span: it is denied, because its truth would be too discomforting
nodes.status_reason: application of the denial thesis n8 to n30

nodes.statement: Evidence that the novelties are radical will be supplied by explaining strange phenomena as doomed efforts at hiding or denying the unfamiliar.
nodes.span: explaining a number of otherwise strange phenomena as frantic —but, as we now know, doomed— efforts at hiding
nodes.status_reason: method chosen to discharge the evidential promise n1 using n8

nodes.statement: Software engineering is doomed because its charter is the self-contradictory "How to program if you cannot".
nodes.span: software engineering has accepted as its charter "How to program if you cannot."
nodes.status_reason: asserted from reading the literature; no derivation given

nodes.statement: The reassuring name "engineering" functions as primitive name-magic, as shown by a manufacturer renaming all its programmers "software engineers" overnight.
nodes.span: it hired, one night, hundreds of new "software engineers" by the simple device of elevating all its programmers
nodes.status_reason: anecdote offered as evidence of symbolic naming

nodes.statement: Measuring programmer productivity as lines of code produced reflects the illusion that programs are ordinary devices; lines should be booked as spent, not produced.
nodes.span: we should not regard them as "lines produced" but as "lines spent"
nodes.status_reason: instance of the device-analogy denial and of n31

nodes.statement: Testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence, yet software engineers keep refining testing strategies like alchemists.
nodes.span: program testing may convincingly demonstrate the presence of bugs, but can never demonstrate their absence
nodes.status_reason: a well-known remark quoted, not proved here

nodes.statement: The term "software maintenance" makes people believe programs wear out, as with the oil company blaming unmaintained PASCAL.
nodes.span: many people continue to believe that programs —and even programming languages themselves— are subject to wear and tear
nodes.status_reason: anecdote and terminology offered as evidence

nodes.statement: The readiness to blame a lack of "programming tools" rests on a medievally shallow analogy and amounts to snake oil.
nodes.span: the shallowness of the underlying analogy is worthy of the Middle Ages
nodes.status_reason: instance of unwarranted analogy per n10 and n4

nodes.statement: The popularity of Artificial Intelligence is explained by the frightening computer becoming less frightening when used to simulate a familiar noncomputer.
nodes.span: the frightening computer becomes less frightening if it is used only to simulate a familiar noncomputer
nodes.status_reason: application of the flight-to-the-familiar mechanism n6/n8

nodes.statement: All computers can do is manipulate symbols and produce results, in a discrete world whose scale of symbols and manipulations baffles imagination.
nodes.span: the only thing computers can do for us is to manipulate symbols and produce results of such manipulations
nodes.status_reason: rests on the discreteness n30 and the scale n25

nodes.statement: A program is best described as an abstract symbol manipulator that becomes concrete when a computer is supplied to it.
nodes.span: the program is an abstract symbol manipulator, which can be turned into a concrete one by supplying a computer
nodes.status_reason: inversion of the standard description, grounded in n43

nodes.statement: Programs are usefully viewed as elaborate formulae of a formal system, so the programmer's task is to derive that formula.
nodes.span: It really helps to view a program as a formula
nodes.status_reason: follows from the abstract symbol-manipulator conception n44

nodes.statement: Mathematics ignored the programming challenge because programs were far longer formulae than it was used to.
nodes.span: programs were so much longer formulae than it was used to that it did not even recognize them as such
nodes.status_reason: consequence of the formula view n45 plus the scale n25

nodes.statement: The only reliable way to derive a program is by human symbol manipulation, so we build mechanical symbol manipulators by human symbol manipulation.
nodes.span: We know of only one reliable way of doing that, viz. by means of symbol manipulation
nodes.status_reason: asserted as known, no argument for uniqueness

nodes.statement: Computing science is the study of the interplay between mechanized and human symbol manipulation.
nodes.span: computing science is —and will always be— concerned with the interplay between mechanized and human symbol manipulation
nodes.status_reason: closes the circle of n44, n45 and n47

nodes.statement: On this definition "automatic programming" is a contradiction in terms.
nodes.span: it reveals "automatic programming" as a contradiction in terms
nodes.status_reason: immediate corollary of n48

nodes.statement: Computing science is located in the direction of formal mathematics and applied logic, but concerned with effective use of formal methods at a far larger scale.
nodes.span: in the direction of formal mathematics and applied logic, but ultimately far beyond where those are now
nodes.status_reason: placement follows from the symbol-manipulation definition n48

nodes.statement: In the long run computing science will transcend mathematics and logic by realizing part of Leibniz's Dream of symbolic calculation as an alternative to human reasoning.
nodes.span: realizing a significant part of Leibniz's Dream of providing symbolic calculation as an alternative to human reasoning
nodes.status_reason: a projection, not derived from earlier nodes

nodes.statement: This vision meets widespread opposition from mathematicians, business, compulsive programmers, computer engineering, the military, soft sciences and the educational business.
nodes.span: it has met widespread —and sometimes even violent— opposition from all sorts of directions
nodes.status_reason: instances of the general resistance to radical novelty n8

nodes.statement: Educational policy is determined not by scientific considerations from the subject taught but by extra-scientific expectations of students, parents, employers and the university's self-image.
nodes.span: hardly influenced by scientific considerations derived from the topics taught, and almost entirely determined by extra-scientific circumstances
nodes.status_reason: asserted diagnosis, illustrated only by a later quotation

nodes.statement: Flaherty reports that Canada's business elite dismisses traditional academics and intellectuals as irrelevant and powerless.
nodes.span: the business elite dismisses traditional academics and intellectuals as largely irrelevant and powerless
nodes.status_reason: cited quotation supporting n53

nodes.statement: The prediction for computing science education is "business as usual": universities lacking courage to teach hard science and further infantilizing the curriculum.
nodes.span: The universities will continue to lack the courage to teach hard science
nodes.status_reason: follows from the extra-scientific determination of policy n53 and n52

nodes.statement: Suggestion one: stop calling an error a bug, since the animistic metaphor hides that the error is the programmer's own creation and makes wrong programs look "almost correct".
nodes.span: begin with cleaning up our language by no longer calling a bug a bug but by calling it an error
nodes.status_reason: applies the misleading-metaphor thesis n4 to programming vocabulary

nodes.statement: Suggestion two: never refer to parts of programs or equipment in anthropomorphic terms, enforced if necessary by fines.
nodes.span:
never
 refer to parts of programs or pieces of equipment in an anthropomorphic terminology
nodes.status_reason: same anti-metaphor principle extended, and justified by n58

nodes.statement: The anthropomorphic metaphor is a handicap: it has repeatedly caused avoidable confusion and rests on a shallow analogy.
nodes.span: the anthropomorphic metaphor —for whose introduction we can blame John von Neumann— is an enormous handicap
nodes.status_reason: instance of shallow analogy n4, supported by the speaker's encounters

nodes.statement: The personification is misleading because it treats the unfamiliar discrete in terms of the familiar continuous.
nodes.span: it suggests that we can adequately cope with the unfamiliar discrete in terms of the familiar continuous
nodes.status_reason: follows from the discrete/analogue contrast n29–n31

nodes.statement: The personification is paralyzing because, persons acting in time, it forces operational semantics and reasoning about computational behaviours.
nodes.span: its adoption effectively prevents a departure from operational semantics
nodes.status_reason: derived from the temporal character of persons plus n58

nodes.statement: Operational reasoning is a tremendous waste of mental effort.
nodes.span: operational reasoning is a tremendous waste of mental effort
nodes.status_reason: asserted here; its justification comes only with the later example

nodes.statement: To demonstrate something about all elements of a large set it is hopelessly inefficient to treat elements individually; the efficient argument uses the set's definition.
nodes.span: the efficient argument does not refer to individual elements at all and is carried out in terms of the set's definition
nodes.status_reason: the point to be illustrated, stated before its support

nodes.statement: Define Q as the 8x8 square with two opposite corner unit squares removed; its area 62 equals that of 31 dominos, and the theorem is that 31 dominos cannot cover Q.
nodes.span:
the figure 
Q
 cannot be covered by 31 of such dominos
nodes.status_reason: a construction and claim introduced for later use

nodes.statement: One possible proof is to generate all placements of 31 dominos and check that none yields Q, a tremendously laborious job.
nodes.span: generating all possible placements of dominos and verifying for each placement that it does not yield the figure
nodes.status_reason: the exhaustive alternative implied by the restatement of the theorem

nodes.statement: The simple proof colours the paper like a chess board: each domino covers one white and one black square, so any placement covers equal numbers, whereas Q's counts differ by 2.
nodes.span: Colour the squares of the squared paper as on a chess board.
nodes.status_reason: a constructed argument whose steps the reader can follow

nodes.statement: The colouring argument is not only vastly shorter but more powerful, proving the generalization to any rectangle with even sides, for which exhaustive exploration is inadequate.
nodes.span:
it covers the generalization of 
Q
 by replacing the original 8 by 8 square by 
any
 rectangle
nodes.status_reason: comparison of n64 and n65 plus infinitude of rectangles

nodes.statement: The moral: deal with all elements of a set by ignoring them and working with the set's definition.
nodes.span: deal with all elements of a set by ignoring them and working with the set's definition
nodes.status_reason: generalized from the worked example, confirming n62

nodes.statement: Since a program defines the set of its possible computations, meeting a specification should be shown by working with the program text while ignoring its executability.
nodes.span: deal with all computations possible under control of a given program by ignoring them and working with the program
nodes.status_reason: the moral n67 applied to the set of computations

nodes.statement: A programming language with syntax and proof rules is a formal system for which execution is only a model, and formal systems should be treated in their own right, so we should reason about programs without mentioning behaviours.
nodes.span: a formal system for which program execution provides only a model
nodes.status_reason: restates n68 via the formal-system/model relation asserted as well-known

nodes.statement: Hence the anthropomorphic metaphor should be banned in computing science, because operational reasoning is a waste of mental effort.
nodes.span: in computing science the anthropomorphic metaphor should be banned
nodes.status_reason: conclusion from n60, n61 and the technical excursion n67–n69

nodes.statement: A demonstrated educational program visualized features of computations, reinforcing exactly what students must learn to ignore, so it must be expected to cause permanent mental damage.
nodes.span: The system highlighted precisely what the student has to learn to ignore
nodes.status_reason: judged bad by the standard set in n68/n69

nodes.statement: A program by itself is only half a conjecture; the other half is its functional specification, and the programmer's task is to present such conjectures as proven theorems.
nodes.span: all by itself, a program is no more than half a conjecture
nodes.status_reason: follows from the formula/proof view n45 and n68

nodes.statement: Proposed course component one: teach predicate calculus as boolean algebra, drilling manipulation of uninterpreted formulae and renaming true/false as black/white to sever intuition.
nodes.span: we rename the values {true, false} of the boolean domain as {black, white}
nodes.status_reason: implements the blank-mind method n6 and the formal stance n69

nodes.statement: Proposed course component two: teach a small clean imperative language whose every construct's semantics is defined by its proof rules.
nodes.span: the corresponding semantics is defined by the proof rules that go with it
nodes.status_reason: required by treating the language as a formal system n69

nodes.statement: Proposed course component three: require a formal proof that each program meets its formal specification, and ensure the language is unimplemented on campus so students cannot test.
nodes.span: the programming language in question has not been implemented on campus so that students are protected
nodes.status_reason: follows from n72 and the ban on operational reasoning n70

nodes.statement: The proposal is serious and sensible, and is dismissed only by quickly invented invalid reasons because it is too radical for many.
nodes.span: Its only disadvantage is that it is too radical for many
nodes.status_reason: application of the denial thesis n8 to the proposal

nodes.statement: The objection that the proposer is out of touch with the real world fails, since real-world problems are largely those left by refusing effective solutions.
nodes.span: the problems of the real world are primarily those you are left with when you refuse to apply their effective solutions
nodes.status_reason: asserted rebuttal without further support

nodes.statement: The objection that freshmen cannot learn such material is refuted: since the early 80's such a course has been given successfully to hundreds of freshmen each year.
nodes.span: such an introductory programming course has successfully been given to hundreds of college freshmen each year
nodes.status_reason: experiential report offered as refutation

nodes.statement: The objection that the course would frustrate students fails: the manipulation rules are so few and simple that students soon discover an unexpectedly powerful tool.
nodes.span: the rules of manipulation are in this case so few and simple
nodes.status_reason: rests on the simplicity of the boolean-algebra training n73

nodes.statement: Teaching effective formal methods is highly rewarding: within months students gain confident command of a new world and a new dimension of intellectual culture.
nodes.span: Within a few months, they find their way in a new world with a justified degree of confidence
nodes.status_reason: generalizes the teaching experience n78 and n79

nodes.statement: Universities should welcome teaching radical novelties, and their willingness to do so is the main safeguard against dictatorships.
nodes.span: it is their calling to welcome the opportunity to do so
nodes.status_reason: follows from n19 and the rewards n80, though the safeguard claim is asserted
